meta.title: Control Crosswalk Mapper
meta.note: A curated, domain-level crosswalk. Coverage is measured against the requirements this crosswalk maps for each framework, not every clause of the standard. Mapping granularity differs by framework and is stated on each one.

families.name: Core control catalogs
families.blurb: The broad, all-purpose control sets an entire security program is usually measured against.

families.name: Cloud and architecture
families.blurb: Benchmarks and reference architectures for cloud platforms and the way networks are now drawn.

families.name: Sector and technology specific
families.blurb: Standards that only bite in a particular industry or on a particular class of system.

families.name: Threat and weakness catalogs
families.blurb: Adversary behavior and software weakness taxonomies, used to check defenses against what attackers actually do.

families.name: Application and API security
families.blurb: What the software you build and the interfaces you expose are measured against.

families.name: AI governance and security
families.blurb: The fast-moving set of AI-specific standards, regulations, and threat taxonomies.

families.name: Cryptography and post-quantum
families.blurb: The algorithm standards and the migration guidance for getting off the ones quantum computers will break.

families.name: Maturity and workforce
families.blurb: How repeatable the program is and who is supposed to be doing the work.

families.name: Testing methodology
families.blurb: Published method for testing your own defenses so a report can be compared year over year.

families.name: Program-specific models
families.blurb: Engagement models, vendor catalogs, and benchmark sets that belong to a specific program. Structure is in place; content is supplied per engagement.

frameworks.name: NIST CSF 2.0
frameworks.note: Mapped at the subcategory level, the same 106 subcategories this site translates.

frameworks.name: CIS Controls v8
frameworks.note: Mapped at the safeguard level across all three implementation groups.

frameworks.name: ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A
frameworks.note: Mapped to the 93 Annex A controls. Clause 4 to 10 management system requirements are not enumerated here.

frameworks.name: SOC 2 Trust Services Criteria
frameworks.note: Mapped to the common criteria plus availability and confidentiality. The criteria themselves are paywalled.

frameworks.name: PCI DSS v4.0
frameworks.note: Mapped at the twelve top-level requirements, not the several hundred sub-requirements.

frameworks.name: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5
frameworks.note: Mapped to base controls. Control enhancements are not enumerated.

frameworks.name: NIST SP 800-171
frameworks.note: Mapped at the fourteen families, the same ones this site's 800-171 self-assessment is built on.

frameworks.name: CMMC 2.0
frameworks.note: Mapped to the three certification levels and the fourteen domains it inherits from 800-171.

frameworks.name: HIPAA Security Rule
frameworks.note: Mapped to the administrative, physical, and technical safeguard standards.

frameworks.name: CISA Cross-Sector Cybersecurity Performance Goals
frameworks.note: A voluntary floor rather than a full framework, aimed at organizations without a mature program.

frameworks.name: CSA Cloud Controls Matrix v4
frameworks.note: Mapped at the seventeen domains. The full matrix has 197 control objectives beneath them.

frameworks.name: CIS Amazon Web Services Foundations Benchmark
frameworks.note: Mapped at the benchmark's five sections, not the individual recommendations, which change with the platform.

frameworks.name: CIS Microsoft Azure Foundations Benchmark
frameworks.note: Mapped at the benchmark's service sections, not the individual recommendations.

frameworks.name: NIST SP 800-207 Zero Trust Architecture
frameworks.note: An architecture document, not a control catalog. Mapped to its seven tenets and three logical components.

frameworks.name: IEC 62443 industrial automation and control systems
frameworks.note: Mapped to the seven foundational requirements plus the security program and secure development parts.

frameworks.name: CIS Oracle Database Benchmark
frameworks.note: Mapped at the benchmark's five sections. Oracle DBSAT and CIS-CAT are the tools that assess against it.

frameworks.name: Telecom network and AI security baselines
frameworks.note: Mapped at the document level: 3GPP TS 33.501 and TS 33.117, GSMA NG.127 and FS.31. Clause-level detail is behind member access.

frameworks.name: MITRE ATT&CK Enterprise
frameworks.note: Mapped to ATT&CK mitigations, the control-shaped layer of the matrix, rather than to tactics or techniques.

frameworks.name: MITRE ATLAS
frameworks.note: Mapped to the sixteen adversarial AI tactics this site already translates in plain English.

frameworks.name: CWE Top 25 Most Dangerous Software Weaknesses
frameworks.note: A ranked weakness list, not a control set. Useful as a target list for what secure development has to prevent.

frameworks.name: OWASP Software Assurance Maturity Model
frameworks.note: Mapped to the fifteen security practices. Each has three maturity levels beneath it.

frameworks.name: OWASP API Security Top 10
frameworks.note: A risk list for machine-to-machine interfaces.

frameworks.name: OWASP Non-Human Identity Top 10
frameworks.note: A risk list for service accounts, tokens, keys, and workload identities.

frameworks.name: NIST AI Risk Management Framework
frameworks.note: Mapped to the nineteen subcategories of Govern, Map, Measure, and Manage that this site translates.

frameworks.name: ISO/IEC 42001:2023 AI management system
frameworks.note: Mapped at the clause level plus Annex A, matching this site's plain-English translation.

frameworks.name: EU Artificial Intelligence Act
frameworks.note: Mapped to the obligation articles that translate into controls. Obligations phase in through 2027 and depend on your role and risk class.

frameworks.name: OWASP Top 10 for Large Language Model Applications
frameworks.note: A risk list for generative AI applications, translated in plain English on this site.

frameworks.name: OWASP Agentic AI threats and mitigations
frameworks.note: Fifteen agent-specific threats. The closest thing to a published capability model for agentic AI security.

frameworks.name: NIST post-quantum standards and migration guidance
frameworks.note: The algorithm standards plus the migration and transition guidance that tells you what to do with them.

frameworks.name: CMMI maturity levels
frameworks.note: A generic process maturity scale. Mapped to the five levels, not to CMMI practice areas.

frameworks.name: NICE Workforce Framework for Cybersecurity
frameworks.note: Mapped to the seven work role categories. Task, knowledge, and skill statements sit beneath them.

frameworks.name: Penetration testing methodology
frameworks.note: The two published methods most network penetration test reports are structured around.

frameworks.name: BastionOne engagement model
frameworks.note: Engagement phases, deliverables, and the recon methodology behind a network penetration test.

frameworks.name: QuiltWorks coalition framework
frameworks.note: Shared-defense structure for organizations pooling security capability.

frameworks.name: Frontier AI readiness framework
frameworks.note: Readiness tiers for organizations adopting frontier-scale AI capability.

frameworks.name: Falcon module catalog
frameworks.note: Platform module coverage mapped to the control domains each module actually satisfies.

frameworks.name: M&A vendor portfolio
frameworks.note: Acquired-company tool overlap, consolidation candidates, and contract timing.

frameworks.name: Fisher Phillips AI legal checklist
frameworks.note: Six employment and workplace law checkpoints for deploying AI on staff or candidates.

frameworks.name: Accenture telecom AI testing framework
frameworks.note: Seven test dimensions for AI deployed in telecom networks, used alongside GSMA NG.127.

signals.name: CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog
signals.what: The authoritative list of vulnerabilities with confirmed in-the-wild exploitation, with remediation due dates for federal agencies.

signals.name: FIRST Exploit Prediction Scoring System
signals.what: A daily-updated probability that a given vulnerability will be exploited in the next 30 days. Pairs with KEV to rank what is left.

signals.name: CVSS severity scoring
signals.what: Severity of a vulnerability if exploited. On its own it is a poor queue, which is why KEV and EPSS exist.

signals.name: Oracle Database Security Assessment Tool
signals.what: Oracle's own assessment tool. Produces the findings a CIS Oracle benchmark review is usually built on.

signals.name: CIS-CAT Pro Assessor
signals.what: Automated scoring of a system against a CIS Benchmark, which is how benchmark coverage gets measured rather than asserted.

signals.name: CycloneDX cryptographic bill of materials
signals.what: A machine-readable inventory of the cryptography a system uses. The starting artifact for any post-quantum migration plan.

signals.name: Software bill of materials
signals.what: The dependency inventory that makes supply chain questions answerable in hours instead of weeks.

signals.name: Industry peer benchmark data
signals.what: Analyst and survey data on what comparable organizations spend, staff, and achieve. Licensed content, supplied per engagement.

signals.name: Consulting cost benchmarks
signals.what: Typical market rates and effort ranges for assessment, testing, and advisory work. Supplied per engagement.

controls.summary: Roles, policies, risk appetite, and oversight that steer the whole program.
Proving the program works to auditors, regulators, and customers.
Measuring how repeatable the program is and comparing it against peers and a target state.
Tracking the laws, contracts, and employment rules that bind how you use technology and AI.
A current inventory of the hardware, software, and data you have to protect.
Knowing what data you hold, how sensitive it is, and guarding it through its life.
Handling personal data lawfully: purpose, consent, retention, and the rights people can exercise.
Managing the risk that vendors and partners introduce.
Learning about threats and giving outsiders a way to report weaknesses.
Finding weaknesses and fixing or patching them on a schedule.
Fixing first what is actually being exploited, using known-exploited and exploit-likelihood signals rather than severity alone.

controls.domain: Shadow IT and Shadow AI Discovery
controls.summary: Finding the tools, SaaS accounts, and AI services people adopted without telling anyone.
Diligence before a deal and safe network, identity, and vendor integration after it.
Granting, reviewing, and revoking access so people reach only what they should.
Proving who a user is, including multi-factor authentication and credential hygiene.
Extra control over admin and other high-power accounts.
Governing the service accounts, API keys, tokens, and workload identities that now outnumber your people.
Deciding access per request from identity, device, and context instead of trusting the network.
Controlling traffic and separating the network so a breach cannot spread freely.
Holding cloud accounts and subscriptions to a published benchmark and catching drift from it.
Protecting laptops, servers, and mobile devices, and stopping malicious code.
Shipping and keeping systems in a locked-down, known-good state.
Hardening the database itself: parameters, listeners, privileges, native auditing, and encryption at rest.

controls.domain: OT and Industrial Control System Security
controls.summary: Protecting plant and process networks where safety and availability outrank confidentiality.
Encrypting data at rest and in transit, and managing the keys behind it.
Inventorying quantum-vulnerable algorithms, building a cryptographic bill of materials, and planning the migration to the new standards.
Filtering the two channels attackers use most: email and the browser.
Protecting facilities, equipment, and the people in them.
Building and running software so it does not ship exploitable flaws.
Protecting the machine-to-machine interfaces: authorization per object, inventory, and rate limits.
Measuring and raising how consistently security practice is built into how software gets made.
Reviewing and controlling changes so they do not break security.
Paying someone to attack you on purpose, with a defined method and a report you act on.
An inventory of AI use, a named owner for each one, a risk tier, and a gate before it goes live.
Measuring an AI system for accuracy, robustness, bias, and abuse before and after release.

controls.domain: Model and Training Data Supply Chain
controls.summary: Knowing where models, weights, datasets, and AI dependencies came from and whether they were tampered with.
Guardrails around a live AI application: input handling, output handling, retrieval boundaries, and usage limits.

controls.domain: Agentic AI and Autonomous Action Control
controls.summary: Constraining what an AI agent may do on its own: tool permissions, its own identity, memory integrity, and a human stop.
Collecting logs and watching for the signs of an attack in progress.
A plan and a team to detect, contain, and recover from incidents.
Reliable, tested backups you can actually restore from.
Keeping critical operations running through disruption.
Teaching people to recognize and resist the attacks aimed at them.
Screening, agreements, and offboarding across the employment life cycle.
Defining security work roles, the skills each needs, and how you hire and grow into them.
